title: SOH, LOH, POH and regions
sub: Where an object lands and how the heap is built physically
cards/0/title: The managed heap is several heaps
cards/0/body:
You saw generations 0, 1 and 2 in the .NET under the hood course. Physically, different heaps with different rules stand behind them:

  • SOH (small object heap) — ordinary objects, generations 0–2. The collector compacts it, sliding live objects together;
  • LOH (large object heap) — objects of 85,000 bytes and more. Collected only together with generation 2, not compacted by default;
  • POH (pinned object heap, .NET 5) — objects that never move;
  • the non-GC heap (.NET 8) — objects the collector never collects at all.

Your code allocates in generation 0, in the LOH or in the POH. Objects get into generations 1 and 2 only by surviving a collection.
cards/0/deep: In the GC sources the LOH and POH together are called the UOH (user old heap): objects there are "old" from birth and are collected together with generation 2. That is why GC.GetGeneration returns 2 for them right away. In the internal numbering the LOH is generation 3 and the POH is 4.
cards/1/title: The threshold is the object size, not the length
cards/1/body:
An object goes to the LOH when its full size — header, type pointer and length included — is at least 85,000 bytes. For a byte[] the bookkeeping is 24 bytes, so the boundary is a length of 84,976:

  • new byte[84_976] — exactly 85,000 bytes → LOH;
  • new byte[84_975] — 84,999 → SOH;
  • new string('x', 50_000) — 22 + 100,000 → LOH.

With collections it is often not the object itself that is large but its internal array: a List<int> is small, but its int[] of 30,000 elements is already in the LOH.
cards/1/code:
Console.WriteLine(GC.GetGeneration(new byte[84_975])); // 0: SOH
Console.WriteLine(GC.GetGeneration(new byte[84_976])); // 2: straight to the LOH
cards/1/deep: The threshold is configurable: System.GC.LOHThreshold in runtimeconfig.json (.NET Core 3.0+), and only upwards from the default. The effective value is visible in GC.GetConfigurationVariables() under the name LOHThreshold. The number 85,000 came from performance tuning, it is not a power of two.
cards/2/q: What goes straight to the LOH? Select all.
cards/2/options/4: The internal array of new List<int>(30_000)
cards/2/explain: byte[84_990] is 85,014 bytes. A 45,000-character string is 90,022. The list's array is an int[30,000], 120,024 bytes. But int[20,000] and long[10,000] are 80,024 bytes each — that is the SOH.
cards/3/title: The LOH is not compacted — by default
cards/3/body:
Moving objects of a hundred kilobytes and more is expensive, so in the LOH the collector does a sweep: dead objects become free blocks, and a free list is built from them. A new large object looks for a fitting gap there. If the gaps are smaller than needed, memory grows even though there is plenty of free space in total. That is fragmentation.

You can compact the LOH on demand: GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode = CompactOnce. The next blocking generation 2 collection compacts the LOH, and the mode switches back to Default by itself.
cards/3/deep: The mode appeared in .NET Framework 4.5.1. The runtime may also compact the LOH on its own: for example, when System.GC.ConserveMemory is set (.NET 6+, values 1–9) and fragmentation is too high. But the best remedy is not to create large temporary arrays: rent them from ArrayPool<T>. More on that in the "Allocation" unit.
cards/4/q: Ask for the LOH to be compacted at the next full collection, and run it
cards/4/explain: The enum has only two values: Default and CompactOnce. There is no "always compact" — the mode is one-shot and resets after the collection.
cards/5/title: POH: a heap for pinned objects
cards/5/body:
Native code and devices need a buffer address that will not move. You can pin an object in the SOH — fixed or GCHandle.Alloc(..., Pinned) — but it becomes a rock in the middle of generation 0: the collector cannot move it or compact the memory around it.

The POH (.NET 5) solves this: objects there never move, so there is no need to pin them. To allocate an array in the POH — GC.AllocateArray<T>(length, pinned: true), or GC.AllocateUninitializedArray<T>(length, pinned: true) without zeroing.

The POH is collected together with generation 2 and is not compacted. It suits long-lived I/O buffers, not short-lived temporary ones.
cards/5/deep: In .NET 5–7, with pinned: true the type T could not be a reference type or contain references; since .NET 8 the restriction is gone. The API offers arrays only — you cannot allocate an ordinary object in the POH. A separate POH limit under a hard heap limit is set with System.GC.HeapHardLimitPOH.
cards/6/q: A 4 KB buffer lives for the whole lifetime of a service, and its address is constantly passed to native I/O. How should you allocate it?
cards/6/options/1: new byte[4096] and GCHandle.Alloc(buf, GCHandleType.Pinned) forever
cards/6/options/2: new byte[100_000] so it lands in the LOH — nothing moves there
cards/6/explain: The POH was made exactly for this: the object never moves and does not get in the way of compacting generation 0.
cards/6/wrong/1: It works, but a pinned object in the SOH gets in the way of compaction and fragments the young generations until it is promoted to generation 2.
cards/6/wrong/2: The LOH is not compacted only by default: CompactOnce or ConserveMemory can move it. Only pinning or the POH guarantee an object stays put.
cards/6/wrong/3: The stack does not outlive the method, and you cannot hand it to asynchronous I/O.
cards/7/body:
Before .NET 7 the heap was made of segments — large chunks of address space. Generations 0 and 1 lived together in one "ephemeral" segment, generation 2 and the LOH in their own. Free space inside a segment could not be given to another generation. A segment went back to the OS only when it became completely empty; otherwise only the tail after the last live object was released.

Since .NET 7, on 64-bit Windows and Linux the heap is made of regions: small blocks, by default 4 MB for the SOH and 32 MB for the LOH and POH. Each region belongs to one generation. Regions that survived a collection can be "promoted" to an older generation as a whole, and empty ones go back to a shared list to be given to any generation or to the OS.

As in the "Memory through the OS’s eyes" unit: at startup the GC reserves a large address range for regions — 256 GB by default — but commits memory only as needed.
cards/7/deep: The range is visible in GC.GetConfigurationVariables() as GCRegionRange; with a hard heap limit it is smaller — five times the limit. The region size is changed with DOTNET_GCRegionSize (.NET 7+) or System.GC.RegionSize in runtimeconfig.json (.NET 10). An object larger than a region gets a region of its own size. In .NET 7 the old segments implementation shipped as a separate clrgc library that could be plugged in with DOTNET_GCName in case of regressions.
cards/8/q: A .NET 8 service on Linux without memory limits. top shows a VIRT of over 256 GB for the process, while RES is 300 MB. What is it?
cards/8/options/0: The GC reserved an address range for regions — this is not used memory
cards/8/options/2: The service allocated 256 GB in the POH
cards/8/explain: A reservation of addresses costs nothing physically, as we covered in the "Memory through the OS’s eyes" unit. Used memory is RES and committed pages, not VIRT.
cards/8/wrong/1: A leak would grow RES and the heap size, not just the virtual address space.
cards/9/title: The non-GC heap: frozen segments in .NET 8
cards/9/body:
Some objects live until the process ends and hold no references the GC needs to know about. In .NET 8 the runtime puts them on the non-GC heap (also called frozen): the collector neither collects nor moves it. It holds:

  • string literals;
  • the Type objects returned by typeof(T);
  • empty arrays from Array.Empty<T>();
  • the boxes of static struct fields without references.

The win is in machine code: the address of such an object never changes, and the JIT bakes it right into the instruction, without a read through an intermediate cell.
cards/9/deep: This is a documented .NET 8 change: GC.GetGeneration may return int.MaxValue for objects on the non-GC heap — do not use the result as an array index. What exactly goes there is an implementation detail: for example, typeof for a type from a collectible context does not, otherwise the type could never be unloaded. The idea grew out of Native AOT's frozen segments, where such objects are prepared at build time.
cards/10/q: Where does the object land in .NET 8+?
cards/11/explain: a is 0, b (LOH) and c (POH) are 2: these heaps are collected together with generation 2. The literal lives on the non-GC heap, and GetGeneration returns int.MaxValue for it.
